title: InfinityStar: Uniﬁed Spacetime AutoRegressive Modeling for Visual Generatio

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The prose states that clips are generated sequentially and are conditioned on prior clips: “clips are generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions.” However, Eq. (2) factorizes each clip as p(r_k^c | r_1^c, ..., r_{k-1}^c, psi(t)) and contains no tokens from c-1 or any earlier clip. As written, clips are conditionally independent given the text and cannot implement the claimed temporal inter-clip autoregression, video extrapolation, or the later attention mechanism that attends to the preceding clip.

The paper defines N in Section 3.2 as the number of sequential clips in a video, then says semantic scale repetition repeats the first Ks scale tuples “N times.” This would make the number of within-clip refinement passes depend on the number of video clips/duration. In contrast, Section 4.1 states that the first 7 scales are repeated 6 times. These are incompatible definitions unless a separate repetition-count variable was intended.

predicted_errors.error_location: Method section structure, between Sections 2.3 and 3.2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript jumps directly from an unheaded paragraph describing “Infinity for Image Generation” to Section 3.2. Section 3.1 is absent, despite the later method referring to Fig. 1 and relying on the image-pyramid/token-block setup. This is not merely numbering style: a necessary method section appears to be missing or misplaced under Related Work, leaving the method organization and specification incomplete.

The first conclusion is interrupted mid-sentence: “By seamlessly integrating spatial and”. It is then followed by a second “## Experiments” block containing Fig. 8 and Tables 4–6, followed by a duplicate “## Conclusion” that begins a different conclusion paragraph. Results and ablations are thus placed after an incomplete conclusion, and the paper contains duplicate conclusion headings. The document must be restored/reordered before it can be reviewed as a coherent paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1, Datasets and Model and Training
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper explicitly leaves core reproduction information unspecified: it gives approximately 221M samples but no train/validation split, gives a 16M-video subset without distributions or balancing criteria, and states that Adam momentum and weight decay are unspecified. It also says global batch sizes and learning-rate schedules are “as detailed,” but supplies no such details in the provided paper. These omissions prevent reconstruction of the training protocol and fair comparison.

InfinityStar’s 83.74 result is explicitly obtained “with prompt rewriting applied,” while the paper acknowledges that “other baselines have variable usage of prompt enhancements.” There is no standardized prompt-rewriting protocol, no rewritten prompts, and no matched no-rewrite result for InfinityStar. Thus the reported ranking is not a controlled comparison, particularly for the claimed margin over HunyuanVideo (83.74 versus 83.24).

The abstract and introduction claim approximately a 10× latency reduction relative to leading diffusion methods, including a claim using tokenizers of the same compression rate. The only presented end-to-end 720p diffusion comparison, Table 6, reports Wan 2.1 at 1864 s and InfinityStar at 58 s, i.e. about 32×. No experiment supporting the quoted 10× matched-compression claim is provided, nor is the comparator for that number identified. The paper must either report the underlying matched protocol/results or revise the quantitative claim.

The paper presents end-to-end latency and speedup claims while saying only that measurements used “a single GPU”; it does not identify the GPU, precision, memory/offloading configuration, decoding settings, sampling settings, or whether each baseline was run under matched software conditions. It instead says Wan and Nova were run with their “default GitHub configurations,” which is not a controlled benchmark. Further, the Table 6 note says baselines were evaluated at different resolutions, whereas every row in the table lists 720p. This makes the comparison and its stated caveat internally unclear.

Table 2 labels a baseline “VideoCrafter-2.0 [5],” but Reference [5] is titled “VideoCrafter1: Open diffusion models for high-quality video generation” (arXiv:2310.19512). VideoCrafter2 is a distinct work/version. The cited source therefore does not identify the baseline named in the table, making the provenance of the reported comparison incorrect.

The paper identifies [38] as the VBench benchmark, but Reference [38] is “Evaluation Agent: Efficient and Promptable Evaluation Framework for Visual Generative Models,” arXiv:2412.09645. The established VBench benchmark is a different work (“VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models,” arXiv:2311.17982). The benchmark attribution should be corrected and the exact VBench version/protocol used must be specified.

The model is trained on approximately 221M image/video samples, including “vendor suppliers” and unspecified “internal collections,” but the paper provides no statement about licenses, consent, privacy handling, rights to use vendor/internal material, filtering of personal or copyrighted content, or data-governance review. For a large-scale image/video generative model, especially one trained on nonpublic collections, this omission prevents assessment of legal and human-subject/data-provenance risks.
